transcript.content: Hi, it's good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, I guess... I guess what brings me here is that my talking gets all mixed up. That's what they tell me anyway. People say they can't follow what I'm saying, but to me, it makes perfect sense, you know? Like, I try to explain about the keys—the keys to the building where I clean, because you have to have the right keys to get into the right rooms, especially after hours when the lights are low and the hum of the vending machines is the only thing you hear. And then, naturally, that makes me think about the jail, because locks and keys, they're the same thing, right? I was thinking about the bars on the windows and how they keep you in, but they also keep things out. And from there, it just flows right into the prayer rug. You have to understand the prayer rug, because it's about patterns and kneeling, and finding a space that's yours when you're locked in or locked out. It's all connected, just like the chess pieces. The knights and the pawns, they all move in specific ways, just like how I have to move through the hallways with my mop bucket. But when I try to lay it all out for people, to show them how the keys and the jail and the rug and the chess pieces are all part of the same big picture, they just look at me blankly. They say I'm jumping around, that my words are a jumble. But I'm just trying to give them the whole story, every detail, because if you miss one part, the rest of it falls apart. So, yeah, I'm here because apparently, I can't explain things right, even though I'm trying as hard as I can to make them see it.
Do you believe that anyone is trying to harm you or plot against you?

Well, harm me... plot against me... it's a strong word, plot, but yes, I do. I really do. It's the building people, the ones who work in the offices during the day while I'm mostly there at night, but sometimes our shifts overlap, you know? And it's not just a feeling, it's a knowing. I know they've marked me. They have this system, this whole intricate system of communicating about me. It's the hallway lights. Sometimes they flicker in this very specific rhythm when I walk past the third-floor conference room—tap, tap, pause, tap—and I know that's them signaling that I'm on the move. And it's the looks, too. These little, sharp glances they give each other when I'm emptying the shredder bins. They think I don't see, but I see everything. I see the way the accountant on the fourth floor adjusts his tie exactly when I walk in, and then the receptionist coughs twice. It's a warning system. They're warning each other about me. 

I even tried to prove it. I went to my supervisor, Mr. Henderson—he's been there fifteen years, always wears these scuffed brown shoes—and I told him, I said, "Mr. Henderson, you have to look at the security cameras. You have to see what they're doing with the lights and the looks." And he did. He brought me into his little office by the loading dock, and he played the tape back. He showed me the hallway, and he said, "Look, there's nothing there. The lights are fine. No one is looking at you." He pointed right at the screen, right at the timestamp. But... but even when he showed me that, even when the screen looked normal to him, I still felt it. I still felt absolutely sure that they had marked me. The camera just couldn't pick up the frequency of it, or maybe they altered the tape. Because I know what I see, and I know they're using the lights and those little looks to keep tabs on me, to plot whatever it is they're planning to do. It's all part of it.
Have you had a period when you felt extremely up or unusually energetic for several days?

Well, up... energetic... yes, yes, I suppose you could say that. There are these times, and it's not just a little bit of energy, it's like a whole current running through me, like the main power line to the industrial buffers we use on the lobby floors. When it hits me, I feel... I feel so high up, like I'm standing on the roof of the building looking down at everything, and I'm just so powerful. I get to laughing, just this loud, booming laugh that echoes all the way down the corridors, and I want to talk to everyone. I'll be pushing my cart and I'll see the night watchman, or maybe one of the late-night executives getting coffee, and I just start talking, loud and fast, telling them about the grand scheme of things, because suddenly I understand it all, right? I feel like I could clean the whole twenty-story building in an hour and still have time to reorganize the supply closets. 

But then... the thing is, if they don't get it, or if they look at me wrong—like if the watchman says, "Hey buddy, keep it down," or if someone questions why I'm talking so loud—it just flips. It flips so fast. It's like a circuit breaker tripping. One second I'm on top of the world, and the next, I just snap. I'll start shouting, really shouting, over the smallest little thing. Like if they ask why I haven't emptied a specific trash can yet, I'll just explode. I'll yell about how they don't understand the sequence, how they can't see the power I have in that moment. It's a very intense feeling, being that high up and then having someone try to pull you down. It's just... it's a lot of energy, a lot of power, and it has to go somewhere, you know?
During those high-energy times, do you need much less sleep than usual?

Sleep? Oh, sleep is... well, during those times, sleep is just a waste. It's a complete waste of time. I mean, why would I lay there in the dark when my brain is firing on all cylinders, right? It's like... it's like the whole world is asleep, but I'm the only one awake, the only one who really sees what's going on. I'll lay down for maybe two, three hours tops. Two or three hours, that's it. And it's not even a deep sleep, it's just a resting of the eyes, really. 

And then, boom, I'm up. I'm up before the sun even thinks about coming up, before the first delivery trucks even hit the loading dock out back. And I don't feel tired. That's the crazy part, I don't feel tired at all. I feel completely fresh, like I just slept for a week. I'll get up, make a pot of coffee—strong, black, the way you need it when you're doing real work—and I just start planning. I start mapping out the whole shift in my head. I'll think, okay, I'll tackle the fourth floor first, get those shredder bins emptied before the accountant even gets his shoes tied, then I'll move down to the lobby, buff the floors till they shine like glass, and I still have time to reorganize the supply closet on the second floor, the one with the broken hinge on the door that no one ever fixes. 

I'll just be sitting there at my kitchen table, going over the schedules, the routes, the inventory of the cleaning supplies, figuring out how to make everything perfectly efficient. Because when I'm like that, I don't need sleep. Sleep is for the people who work in the offices during the day, the ones who need eight hours just to sit at a desk and stare at a computer. But me? I've got the energy, I've got the power. I don't need it. I can just keep going and going, like a machine that never needs to be plugged in. It's just two or three hours, and then I'm ready to take on the whole building, the whole world, really.
Have there been times when you were not feeling especially high or full of energy, but still believed the building people were signaling about you?

Oh, absolutely. Yes. It’s not just when my engine is running hot, you know, not just when I've got all that electricity in me. There are plenty of times... well, there was this one stretch, these calmer weeks, really. I wasn't feeling all high and mighty, and I wasn't feeling dragged down into the dirt either. I wasn't deeply depressed or anything, just... just regular. Punching in, doing my floors, punching out. 

But the thing is, doctor, even when I'm feeling perfectly steady like that, the signaling doesn't stop. It never really stops. I remember this one period, it went on for more than two weeks straight during that calm spell, where I still knew exactly what they were doing. The office people, they were still doing the taps, the looks, the coughs. And... well, it’s not just them, actually. It’s the vents, too. During that whole time, that whole two-week period when I was feeling totally level, I still heard him. The man in the vents. 

It’s the big HVAC ducts, the square aluminum ones that run right over the dropped acoustic tiles in the main corridors. You can hear the air rushing, sure, but underneath the air,
When you were feeling level, did you still hear the man in the vents talking to you?

Yes, yes, exactly. The man in the vents. It doesn't matter if I'm feeling level or not, he's still there. I'll be in the mop closet, you know, the one on the third floor near the freight elevator, mixing the floor cleaner—just the right ratio, you can't use too much or it leaves a sticky film—and I'll hear him. Clear as day. It's not a mumble, it's not the wind. It's a man's voice. 

He'll say my name. Just... call out my name, echoing down through the aluminum ductwork. Or sometimes, and this is the part that really gets to me, he'll tell me I ruined everything. "You ruined everything," he says. Over and over. And I'm just standing there with my hand on the mop handle, looking around, because it sounds... Doctor, it sounds exactly like there is a man standing right beside me, right over my shoulder in that tiny closet. 

I'll even turn around, I'll drop the mop and look behind the utility sink, thinking maybe one of the maintenance guys snuck in there to mess with me. But there's never anyone there. Just the cinderblock walls and the smell of industrial pine cleaner. But the voice, it's so real. It's got a deep pitch to it, kind of gravelly, like someone who's been smoking for forty years. And he just keeps telling me I ruined it all, even when I'm just trying to do my job, even when I'm feeling perfectly fine and just trying to get the scuff marks off the linoleum. It's just... it's impossible to ignore when it sounds that real, you know? Like he's right there in the room with me.
For at least one month, have you been hearing the man in the vents or believing the building people were signaling about you?

A month? Oh, doctor, a month would be a vacation. A month would be nothing. No, no, it's been... well, let me think. It started way before the winter holidays last year, because I remember the salt on the sidewalks and how the lobby floors were constantly a mess, and I was already hearing him then. And the people in the offices, the signaling, that started right around the same time. 

So, it's been... it's been about a year and a half. A solid year and a half of this. Every day, every single shift. It doesn't matter if it's a Tuesday or a Friday, if I'm on the day shift filling in or doing my regular night rotation. For eighteen months, I've had to walk into that building knowing they're watching me, knowing they've got some kind of system figured out to keep tabs on me. The coughs, the way they shift their chairs when I walk by with the trash cart... all of it. And the voice in the vents, that gravelly voice telling me I ruined everything, that's been there the whole time, too. A year and a half of looking over my shoulder, of checking the grates, of trying to figure out what I'm supposed to have ruined. It's exhausting, doctor, it really is. You try buffing a thousand square feet of marble while a man in the ceiling is whispering at you for a year and a half straight. It changes how you do your job, it changes how you walk down a hallway. You start stepping quieter, you know? Trying not to trigger whatever it is they're signaling about. So, yes, much longer than a month. A year and a half, at least.

I'll even turn around, I'll drop the mop and look behind the utility sink, thinking maybe one of the maintenance guys snuck in there to mess with me. But there's never anyone there. Just the cinderblock walls and the smell of industrial pine cleaner. But the voice, it's so real. It's got a deep pitch to it, kind of gravelly, like someone who's been smoking for forty years. And he just keeps telling me I ruined it all, even when I'm just trying to do my job, even when I'm feeling perfectly fine and just trying to get the scuff marks off the linoleum. It's just... it's impossible to ignore when it sounds that real, you know? Like he's right there in the room with me.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms have persisted for at least one month, which would help distinguish schizophrenia from schizoaffective disorder and bipolar I disorder with psychotic features.
doctor.question: For at least one month, have you been hearing the man in the vents or believing the building people were signaling about you?

target_item.name: Psychotic Symptoms Duration
target_item.manifestation: The voices and fixed worries about being watched or marked have been with me for about a year and a half.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the duration of the psychotic symptoms (hearing voices and believing people are signaling), which corresponds to the 'Psychotic Symptoms Duration' item.

patient.answer:
A month? Oh, doctor, a month would be a vacation. A month would be nothing. No, no, it's been... well, let me think. It started way before the winter holidays last year, because I remember the salt on the sidewalks and how the lobby floors were constantly a mess, and I was already hearing him then. And the people in the offices, the signaling, that started right around the same time. 

So, it's been... it's been about a year and a half. A solid year and a half of this. Every day, every single shift. It doesn't matter if it's a Tuesday or a Friday, if I'm on the day shift filling in or doing my regular night rotation. For eighteen months, I've had to walk into that building knowing they're watching me, knowing they've got some kind of system figured out to keep tabs on me. The coughs, the way they shift their chairs when I walk by with the trash cart... all of it. And the voice in the vents, that gravelly voice telling me I ruined everything, that's been there the whole time, too. A year and a half of looking over my shoulder, of checking the grates, of trying to figure out what I'm supposed to have ruined. It's exhausting, doctor, it really is. You try buffing a thousand square feet of marble while a man in the ceiling is whispering at you for a year and a half straight. It changes how you do your job, it changes how you walk down a hallway. You start stepping quieter, you know? Trying not to trigger whatever it is they're signaling about. So, yes, much longer than a month. A year and a half, at least.

inference.note: Psychotic symptoms (auditory hallucinations and persecutory delusions) persist for >2 weeks during a euthymic/level period, ruling out F31.2 and supporting schizoaffective disorder, manic type. Duration and mood-independent psychosis also make F20.0 less likely than F25.0.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has clear psychotic symptoms (persecutory delusions, auditory hallucinations, disorganized speech) plus manic symptoms (elevated/expansive mood, increased energy, decreased need for sleep, loud/rapid talk, irritability). Crucially, psychotic symptoms were explicitly present for more than two weeks during a period when mood was level, which supports schizoaffective disorder, manic type, over bipolar I disorder with psychotic features.
